blocks.text: ABCDE assessment • Emergency response • Team leadership • Structured handover

You are the doctor on duty in the labour ward. A pregnant woman suddenly deteriorates. You are required to assess her, initiate emergency management, delegate tasks and communicate effectively with the obstetric team.
Possible scenarios include:
Postpartum haemorrhage with shock.
Eclampsia.
Maternal sepsis.
Shoulder dystocia.
Umbilical cord prolapse.
Uterine rupture.
Maternal collapse.
Suspected pulmonary embolism.
Fetal bradycardia during labour.
This station tests whether you can recognise a life-threatening emergency, initiate immediate treatment and lead a coordinated team response.
The most important rule: Treat immediate threats to life as you find them. Do not wait to complete the entire history or examination before intervening.

subsections.subsection_title: The first 60 seconds: what to do

blocks.text: When an obstetric emergency occurs, follow this sequence.
Activate the appropriate obstetric emergency response and summon senior obstetric, anaesthetic, midwifery and neonatal support as indicated.
Assess airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, treating immediately life-threatening abnormalities as you identify them.
Assign monitoring, intravenous access, investigations, medication preparation, documentation and emergency equipment.
Use the history, examination and bedside findings to initiate cause-specific treatment without avoidable delay.
Review the response to treatment, escalate early if the patient is deteriorating and arrange definitive care.
Assess whether the woman can speak and maintain her airway.
Look for:
Obstruction.
Reduced consciousness.
Vomit or blood in the airway.
Seizure-related airway compromise.
Actions:
Call for airway assistance if required.
Open and maintain the airway.
Use suction if needed.
Provide appropriate airway adjuncts or advanced airway management through trained personnel.
Protect the cervical spine if trauma is suspected.
In an unconscious pregnant woman, airway management may be complicated by aspiration risk and pregnancy-related airway changes.
Assess:
Respiratory rate.
Oxygen saturation.
Chest movement and air entry.
Work of breathing.
Cyanosis.
Signs of pulmonary oedema or pneumothorax.
Actions:
Give oxygen when indicated by hypoxaemia or critical illness, titrated to an appropriate target.
Support ventilation if necessary.
Investigate and treat the underlying cause.
Consider pulmonary embolism, aspiration, pulmonary oedema or other cardiopulmonary causes when clinically appropriate.
Do not assume that every breathless pregnant woman has asthma or anxiety.
Assess:
Pulse and blood pressure.
Capillary refill and peripheral perfusion.
Skin temperature and colour.
External bleeding.
Uterine tone and vaginal bleeding when relevant.
Urine output and mental status as indicators of perfusion.
Actions:
Obtain large-bore intravenous access where appropriate.
Take blood samples, including full blood count, blood group and crossmatch, coagulation studies or other tests according to the suspected cause.
Initiate appropriate fluid or blood-product resuscitation.
Control haemorrhage if present.
Monitor the response closely.
Involve senior clinicians and critical care early when required.
In pregnancy, a normal-looking blood pressure does not exclude significant haemorrhage. Tachycardia, altered mental state and poor peripheral perfusion may be early signs of deterioration.
Assess:
Level of consciousness using AVPU or Glasgow Coma Scale.
Pupillary response where appropriate.
Blood glucose.
Seizure activity.
Focal neurological deficits.
Severe headache or visual symptoms.
Actions:
Check and correct hypoglycaemia.
Treat seizures according to the suspected cause.
Consider eclampsia, stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, hypoxia and metabolic causes.
Protect the woman from injury during a seizure.
Expose only as much as needed to perform an appropriate examination while preserving dignity and warmth.
Look for:
Vaginal bleeding.
Abdominal tenderness or distension.
Uterine tone.
Surgical wounds or trauma.
Rash or other signs of infection.
Leg swelling when thromboembolism is suspected.
Obstetric findings relevant to the emergency.
Prevent hypothermia, maintain privacy and involve appropriate chaperones for intimate examinations.

subsections.subsection_title: Maternal collapse: cardiac arrest in pregnancy

blocks.text: Maternal cardiac arrest is a time-critical emergency requiring immediate resuscitation.
Suspect cardiac arrest if the woman is unresponsive and is not breathing normally. Check for signs of circulation according to the resuscitation protocol, without delaying chest compressions.
Call the resuscitation team and activate the maternal cardiac arrest protocol.
Begin high-quality CPR immediately.
Attach a defibrillator and follow standard rhythm-based resuscitation algorithms.
Give indicated medications and defibrillation according to the applicable adult advanced life support protocol.
Establish airway management and intravenous or intraosseous access.
Identify and treat reversible causes.
If the uterus is large enough to cause aortocaval compression, perform manual left uterine displacement while maintaining effective chest compressions.
Prepare for resuscitative delivery when indicated under the maternal cardiac arrest protocol.
Important: Do not delay CPR, defibrillation or other essential resuscitation to perform obstetric manoeuvres.

In maternal cardiac arrest with a uterus large enough to cause aortocaval compression, the team should prepare early for resuscitative delivery if return of spontaneous circulation is not achieved promptly.

The objective is to improve maternal resuscitation as well as potentially benefit the fetus. The procedure should be undertaken at the arrest location when indicated, by a trained team, rather than delaying for transfer to theatre.
The precise timing and technique should follow current resuscitation guidance and the clinical situation.
Consider the usual resuscitation causes, adapted to pregnancy:
Hypovolaemia, including haemorrhage.
Hypoxia.
Metabolic or electrolyte disturbance.
Hypothermia.
Tension pneumothorax.
Cardiac tamponade.
Toxins or medication effects.
Pulmonary or coronary thrombosis.
Also consider pregnancy-specific causes such as amniotic fluid embolism, severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, anaesthetic complications and obstetric haemorrhage.
A strong OSCE candidate does not try to do everything personally.
Use named, direct instructions and confirm that the task has been understood.
Maintain an overview of the patient.
Assign roles.
Make key clinical decisions.
Ensure escalation and reassessment.
Coordinate definitive management.
Record observations.
Establish access and prepare equipment within competence.
Assist with prescribed treatment.
Monitor bleeding, consciousness and urine output as appropriate.
Assist with airway and haemodynamic support.
Provide anaesthesia or advanced resuscitation.
Support intensive care planning.
Arrange blood products and laboratory tests.
Prepare theatre or specialist equipment.
Provide neonatal support when indicated.
Document events and times.
Instead of saying, “Someone get blood,” say:
“Mary, please activate the major haemorrhage protocol and contact the blood bank now. Please repeat back the instruction.”
When the task is completed, the team member should report back:
“The major haemorrhage protocol has been activated, and the blood bank has been contacted.”
This reduces ambiguity and helps the leader maintain situational awareness.
Use SBAR when escalating to a senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, intensive care clinician or another team.
“I am calling about a 32-year-old woman, two hours postpartum, who is deteriorating with heavy vaginal bleeding and signs of shock.”
“She delivered vaginally two hours ago. Her estimated blood loss is increasing, and the uterus is poorly contracted.”
“She is tachycardic and hypotensive. I suspect postpartum haemorrhage with hypovolaemic shock.”
“Please attend immediately. We have activated the haemorrhage protocol and started resuscitation. We need urgent senior review and definitive haemorrhage control.”
SBAR should not delay immediate life-saving action. If the patient is critically unstable, call for emergency assistance while initiating treatment.
A woman develops heavy bleeding immediately after delivery. She becomes pale, tachycardic and hypotensive.
Immediate priorities:
Call for help and activate the haemorrhage protocol.
Assess ABCDE and quantify blood loss.
Begin appropriate resuscitation and obtain intravenous access.
Assess uterine tone, placenta and genital tract for the cause.
Initiate uterine massage and appropriate uterotonics when uterine atony is suspected.
Give tranexamic acid promptly when indicated under the postpartum haemorrhage protocol.
Arrange blood products and correct coagulopathy where necessary.
Escalate to balloon tamponade, surgery or other definitive haemorrhage control if bleeding persists.
Remember the 4 Ts: Tone, Trauma, Tissue and Thrombin.
A pregnant woman with severe hypertension develops a generalised seizure.
Immediate priorities:
Call for help.
Protect her from injury and maintain airway and breathing.
Position laterally when feasible.
Give magnesium sulfate according to the local eclampsia protocol.
Treat severe hypertension with an appropriate agent.
Monitor oxygenation, blood pressure, urine output and magnesium toxicity where indicated.
Assess mother and fetus after stabilisation.
Plan delivery once the mother has been stabilised, according to the clinical situation.
Do not attempt to force anything into the woman's mouth during a seizure.
A woman after delivery has fever, tachycardia, hypotension and altered mental status.
Immediate priorities:
Recognise possible sepsis with organ dysfunction.
Call senior help and assess ABCDE.
Obtain appropriate cultures if doing so does not delay treatment.
Administer prompt intravenous antibiotics according to the local protocol.
Give appropriate intravenous fluids with repeated assessment of response.
Measure lactate and other investigations as indicated.
Identify and control the source of infection.
Escalate to critical care if required.
The fetal heart rate becomes severely abnormal following rupture of membranes, and cord prolapse is identified.
Immediate priorities:
Call for urgent obstetric assistance.
Relieve compression of the cord by elevating the presenting part manually or using another appropriate manoeuvre.
Position the woman to reduce cord compression.
Avoid unnecessary handling of the cord.
Stop oxytocin if it is running.
Expedite delivery, usually by emergency caesarean section unless vaginal birth is immediately achievable and appropriate.
Continue fetal monitoring and communicate clearly with the theatre team.
Do not attempt to push the cord back into the uterus.
The fetal head has delivered, but the shoulders do not deliver with routine gentle traction.
Immediate priorities:
Recognise shoulder dystocia and call for help.
Ask the woman to stop pushing temporarily while the team organises.
Note the time and clearly announce the emergency.
Perform McRoberts manoeuvre and apply suprapubic pressure.
Use further appropriate manoeuvres according to the local protocol and the operator's competence.
Avoid fundal pressure and excessive traction on the fetal head.
Arrange neonatal resuscitation and assess the mother for trauma and haemorrhage after delivery.
In an emergency, prioritise interventions according to the immediate threat.

rows: Activate resuscitation, start CPR and follow cardiac arrest protocol
Seizure with severe hypertension in pregnancy
Airway safety, seizure treatment and urgent blood pressure control
Immediate resuscitation, antibiotics and source control
Call senior obstetric help, identify reversible causes and expedite birth when indicated

blocks.text: In a simulation, verbalise your priorities. For example:
“This patient is haemodynamically unstable. I will call for help, begin ABCDE assessment, establish intravenous access and initiate resuscitation while the team assesses and treats the cause.”

subsections.subsection_title: Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. Why do you use ABCDE?
It provides a systematic approach to identifying and treating immediate life-threatening problems in order of priority, while allowing reassessment after each intervention.
Q2. What is closed-loop communication?
The team leader gives a clear instruction to a named person, that person repeats or acknowledges it, and reports back when the task is completed.
Q3. Why is early escalation important?
It brings additional expertise, equipment and resources to the patient before deterioration becomes irreversible.
Q4. What is the role of the team leader?
To maintain an overview, allocate tasks, make clinical decisions, ensure communication, monitor treatment response and arrange definitive care.
Q5. What is SBAR?
Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation—a structured method for communicating clinical information and requesting assistance.
Q6. Should you finish taking the history before starting treatment?
No. Immediate threats to life should be treated as they are identified. A focused history can be obtained simultaneously by another team member or once the patient is more stable.
Q7. What if the initial treatment is not working?
Reassess ABCDE, reconsider the diagnosis, verify that interventions have been delivered correctly, escalate promptly and move to definitive management according to the relevant emergency protocol.
Q8. Why is documentation important during an emergency?
It records clinical findings, treatment, response, timing, decisions and communication. It also supports continuity of care and later review.
Failing to call for help early.
Completing the history before addressing airway, breathing or circulation.
Giving vague instructions to the team.
Failing to assign a person to record observations and timings.
Not reassessing after treatment.
Delaying definitive treatment while awaiting investigations.
Forgetting to involve anaesthesia, neonatal services or critical care when indicated.
Failing to communicate the working diagnosis and plan.
Neglecting maternal dignity and family communication.
Failing to document the response and outcome.
Recognise deterioration and start ABCDE.
Call senior, anaesthetic and other appropriate teams.
Use named individuals and closed-loop communication.
Treat the cause and organise definitive management.
Repeat observations and reassess ABCDE.
Document actions and communicate using SBAR.
Final OSCE takeaway: In obstetric emergencies, demonstrate early recognition, simultaneous assessment and treatment, clear delegation, repeated reassessment and timely definitive management.
